summary: Specifies a data structure that describes how suitable cryptographic algorithms are for use at a given time, since algorithms weaken over the years. The structure lets software automatically check whether an algorithm is still acceptable when signing, verifying, or encrypting. It is on the standards track.

eli5.summary: Locks get easier to pick as time passes. This format is like a label on each lock saying how safe it still is today, so a computer can decide automatically whether to keep using it.

questions: how to tell if a cryptographic algorithm is still secure
what is a security suitability policy
how are algorithm validity periods expressed
subtitle: A machine-readable policy that says which cryptographic algorithms are still safe to use, and until when.

tldr.problem: Cryptographic algorithms weaken over the years, but expert evaluations of them are published as documents for humans, so software cannot check automatically whether an algorithm was or is suitable at a given time.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a security suitability policy in XML and ASN.1. It lists algorithms, optional parameter constraints such as RSA modulus length, and validity periods, and it can be signed by its publisher. A processing procedure turns a policy, an algorithm and a time of interest into an answer.
tldr.outcome: Signing, verifying, archiving and encryption tools can ask whether an algorithm was suitable at a past, present or future time, though a suitable algorithm does not by itself prove a whole scheme is secure.

today: RFC 5698 is a Proposed Standard from November 2009. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Algorithms Need an Expiry Date
sections.content:
Digital signatures depend on algorithms with certain properties: a hash algorithm must resist collisions, and for public key algorithms, computing the private key from the public key must be infeasible. Computers get faster and cryptography advances, so algorithms or their parameters become insecure over the years. The RFC cites MD5 as unsuitable today for many purposes.

A signature made with a weak algorithm has no probative value, unless it was protected by a strong algorithm before the weak one was considered broken. This matters most for long-term archiving. Evaluations come from expert committees and are published for humans to read, for example by the German Federal Network Agency. DSSC defines a data structure that expresses such evaluations so tools can process them. It does not catalog the security properties of algorithms or say which ones to evaluate.
sections.eli5: A padlock that was safe years ago may be easy to open today. DSSC is a label that tells a computer how long each padlock can be trusted.

sections.title: Requirements and Assumptions
sections.content:
The data structure must allow automatic interpretation, be flexible enough for algorithms not yet known and independent of the intended use, support source authentication (policies from different publishers need not agree, so each must be attributable), and allow integrity and authenticity checks, including the date of issue.

An algorithm is suitable at a time of interest if it is in the current policy, the time falls within its validity period, and any parameters meet the security constraints. A policy is assumed to list all currently known algorithms, including expired ones. Multiple instances of the same algorithm are prohibited. Publishers may extend an algorithm's lifetime by issuing a revised policy but should not resurrect algorithms that have already expired.
sections.eli5: The label has to be easy for a computer to read, say who wrote it, and be hard to fake. It also must never contradict itself.

sections.title: The Policy Data Structure
sections.content:
The root element is SecuritySuitabilityPolicy, in the XML namespace urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:dssc. It holds a PolicyName (a name, with optional OID and URI), a Publisher, a PolicyIssueDate, an optional NextUpdate, an optional human-readable Usage, one or more Algorithm elements and an optional XML Signature.

Each Algorithm has an AlgorithmIdentifier (a human-readable name, at least one OID in dot notation, optional URIs) and one or more Evaluation elements. An Evaluation may carry Parameter constraints and always has a Validity with an optional Start and End date. No end date means open-ended validity. For example, RSA with a 1024-bit modulus may have a different suitability period than RSA with a 2048-bit one.

A Parameter has a name attribute and a Min and/or Max value, with at least one constraint required. The same value in both gives an exact value. The names moduluslength (RSA) and plength and qlength (DSA) SHOULD be used. The optional signature MUST be an enveloped XML signature, and then the policy element MUST have an id attribute for the signature to reference.
sections.eli5: Think of a list of padlock brands. Each entry says how big the lock must be and the last day it counts as safe. At the bottom is the publisher's seal, so you know it is real.

sections.title: XML and ASN.1 Encodings
sections.content:
Policies MUST be expressed in XML or ASN.1, and SHOULD be published in both for interoperability. An XML policy MUST be well-formed and SHOULD be valid, must be based on XML 1.0, and MUST be encoded in UTF-8. It uses the MIME type application/dssc+xml, and its file extension is .xdssc.

An ASN.1 policy file MUST contain only the DER encoding of one policy, with no extra header or trailer. It uses the MIME type application/dssc+der, with file extension .dssc. The ASN.1 modules appear in two syntaxes, 1988 (informative) and 1997 (normative), and the XML schema is in an appendix.
sections.eli5: The same label can be written in two languages, one that people and programs both read easily and one that is more compact. Publishing both helps everyone understand it.

sections.title: How a Tool Evaluates an Algorithm
sections.content:
The inputs are the policy, the current time, the algorithm identifier with any parameter values, and optionally a time of interest. With no time of interest, the tool works out when the algorithm stops being suitable.

First verify the policy. The signature SHOULD be verified and a certification path to a trust anchor SHOULD be validated, using only algorithms that are suitable per the policy itself. If verification fails, the policy MUST be rejected. A NextUpdate in the past also means rejection.

Then find the Algorithm element by matching OIDs. If none matches, the algorithm is unknown. Discard each Evaluation whose Start is after the time of interest or whose End is before it. Next check parameters: discard an evaluation if a required parameter was not supplied, is below Min, is above Max, or fails an unrecognized constraint.

The output is the error "algorithm unknown", the maximum End time (or "algorithm has an indefinite End time") when no time of interest was given, the error "algorithm unsuitable", or the surviving evaluations.
sections.eli5: To check a lock, find its entry in the list, see if today falls inside its safe dates, and make sure your lock is big enough. If all three pass, it is fine to use.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
A wrong policy leads to weak signatures or wrong verification results. Publishers MUST prevent unauthorized manipulation before signing, and there is no mechanism to revoke a published policy, so its lifespan should be chosen with care. Operators SHOULD accept policies only from trusted publishers, SHOULD check certificate status by CRL or OCSP, and MUST NOT allow a policy to be altered or replaced once accepted. They SHOULD check periodically for new policies, and publishers are advised to include NextUpdate.

The RFC warns that the policy covers one algorithm at a time. An unsuitable algorithm does not always make a whole data structure insecure, for instance when a 1024-bit RSA signature was timestamped with a 2048-bit key before the weaker size was broken. In the other direction, a suitable basic algorithm does not make every scheme built on it secure, so a policy SHOULD also evaluate signature schemes. Re-encrypting old documents will not protect ones already intercepted.
sections.eli5: The label is only as good as the person who wrote it, so check who signed it. Even a good lock can be used badly, so one label never tells the whole safety story.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: IANA registered the XML namespace urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:dssc, the schema URN urn:ietf:params:xml:schema:dssc, and the two MIME types. It also created a registry with two sub-registries. Parameter Definitions uses the policy "RFC Required" and starts with moduluslength, plength and qlength. Cryptographic Algorithms uses "First Come First Served" and holds names, OIDs and optional URIs, such as sha-1 with OID 1.3.14.3.2.26, to help when writing a policy.
sections.eli5: There is an official phone book where the names and codes for each lock type are written down so everyone spells them the same way.

viz.caption: STRUCTURE OF A DSSC POLICY (RFC 5698, SECTION 3)

items.title: 1. Verify policy
items.text: Check the signature and certification path, and reject the policy if NextUpdate has passed.

items.title: 2. Check validity
items.text: Match the algorithm by OID and discard evaluations whose Start or End excludes the time of interest.

items.title: 3. Check parameters
items.text: Discard evaluations whose Min, Max or other constraints the supplied values do not meet.
